lessons.title: What are Articles?
lessons.description: Understand the meaning and purpose of articles in English.

sections.heading: 1. What is an Article?
sections.content: An article is a word used before a noun to indicate whether we are referring to something specific or something non-specific.

examples.explanation: A refers to a non-specific dog. The listener does not know which dog.
The refers to the specific dog already mentioned.

sections.heading: 2. Types of Articles
sections.content: English has three articles: A, An and The.

rules.name: A
rules.description: An indefinite article generally used before singular countable nouns beginning with a consonant sound.

rules.name: An
rules.description: An indefinite article generally used before singular countable nouns beginning with a vowel sound.

rules.name: The
rules.description: A definite article used when referring to a specific or identifiable noun.
rules.example: The sun, the book on the table.

sections.heading: 3. Definite and Indefinite Articles
sections.content: A and An are indefinite articles. The is a definite article.

examples.explanation: The dress is not identified specifically.
The dress is now identifiable from the context.

sections.heading: 4. Important Note
sections.content: Articles are generally used with nouns. However, not every noun requires an article. The absence of an article in certain contexts is called the zero article.

examples.explanation: Books refers to books generally, so no article is needed.

lessons.title: Types of Articles
lessons.description: Learn about definite, indefinite and zero articles in English.

sections.heading: 1. The Three Articles
sections.content: English has three articles: A, An and The. They are divided into two main categories: indefinite articles and the definite article.

rules.name: Indefinite Articles
rules.description: A and An are used when referring to a non-specific singular countable noun.

rules.name: Definite Article
rules.description: The is used when referring to a specific or identifiable noun.
rules.example: The bird was sitting on a tree.

sections.heading: 2. Indefinite Articles – A and An
sections.content: A and An introduce a noun that is not specific or has not been identified yet.

rules.name: A
rules.description: Used before a word beginning with a consonant sound.
rules.example: A book, a car, a university.

rules.name: An
rules.description: Used before a word beginning with a vowel sound.
rules.example: An apple, an umbrella, an hour.

sections.heading: 3. Definite Article – The
sections.content: The identifies a particular person, place, animal or thing. It can be used with singular nouns, plural nouns and uncountable nouns when they are specific.

examples.explanation: We are referring to a particular teacher.

examples.sentence: The books on the table are mine.
examples.explanation: We are referring to specific books.

sections.heading: 4. Zero Article
sections.content: Sometimes we do not use any article before a noun. This is called the zero article.

examples.explanation: Dogs refers to animals in general, so no article is required.
Water is used in a general sense, so no article is required.

sections.heading: 5. Quick Comparison
sections.content: Remember the difference between these three forms:

examples.explanation: Any non-specific pen.
A particular pen known to the listener.
Pens in general; no article is needed.

lessons.title: Definite vs Indefinite Articles
lessons.description: Understand when to use A, An and The based on whether a noun is general or specific.

sections.heading: 1. Indefinite Articles – A and An
sections.content: A and An are used when we talk about a singular countable noun that is not specific or is being mentioned for the first time.

examples.sentence: I saw a dog in the park.
examples.explanation: We are mentioning a dog for the first time. The listener does not know which dog.
An is used because umbrella begins with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 2. Definite Article – The
sections.content: The is used when the noun is specific, already known, or identifiable to the speaker and listener.

examples.sentence: I saw a dog. The dog was barking.
examples.explanation: The dog has already been introduced, so we now know which dog is being discussed.
The speaker and listener can identify which door is meant from the situation.

sections.heading: 3. General vs Specific Meaning
sections.content: A or An introduces one non-specific item. The points to a particular item that can be identified.

examples.explanation: Any suitable pen will do. No particular pen is identified.

examples.sentence: I need the pen on your desk.
examples.explanation: A particular pen is identified by its location.

sections.heading: 4. When No Article Is Used
sections.content: Sometimes we use no article before plural or uncountable nouns when speaking generally.

examples.explanation: Books refers to books in general, not particular books.
Water is used in a general sense, so no article is needed.

sections.heading: 5. Quick Comparison
sections.content: Compare these sentences to understand how the article changes the meaning.

examples.explanation: She wants any suitable laptop, not a particular one.

examples.sentence: She wants the laptop we saw yesterday.
examples.explanation: She wants a particular laptop that both people can identify.

lessons.title: Vowel and Consonant Sounds
lessons.description: Learn why the sound at the beginning of a word determines whether we use A or An.

sections.heading: 1. The Basic Rule
sections.content: Use A before a consonant sound and An before a vowel sound. The choice depends on pronunciation, not simply on the first written letter.

examples.explanation: Book begins with the consonant sound /b/.
Apple begins with the vowel sound /æ/.

sections.heading: 2. Vowel Sounds
sections.content: Vowel sounds include sounds commonly represented by A, E, I, O and U. Use An when the next word begins with a vowel sound.

examples.explanation: Egg begins with a vowel sound.
Orange begins with a vowel sound.
Idea begins with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 3. Consonant Sounds
sections.content: Use A when the next word begins with a consonant sound.

examples.explanation: Car begins with the consonant sound /k/.
Teacher begins with the consonant sound /t/.
House begins with the consonant sound /h/.

sections.heading: 4. Words That Begin with U
sections.content: Some words begin with the letter U but have a /y/ sound, like the beginning of the word 'yes'. These take A, not An.

examples.explanation: University begins with the consonant sound /y/.
Useful begins with the consonant sound /y/.
Umbrella begins with a vowel sound.

sections.heading: 5. Silent H Words
sections.content: Some words begin with H, but the H is silent. Use An when the pronounced word begins with a vowel sound.

examples.explanation: The H in hour is silent. The word begins with a vowel sound.
The H in honest is silent.
The H in hotel is pronounced, so it begins with a consonant sound.

sections.heading: 6. Abbreviations and Initialisms
sections.content: For abbreviations read letter by letter, choose A or An based on the sound of the first spoken letter.

examples.explanation: The letter M is pronounced 'em', which begins with a vowel sound.
The letter F is pronounced 'ef', which begins with a vowel sound.
The letter U is pronounced 'you', which begins with a consonant sound.
